name: Romania
summary_text: Romania decriminalised same-sex relations and the practice is legal nationwide. Outright International's country overview records that Government Ordinance 137/2000 prohibits discrimination on grounds of sex and sexual orientation, while institutional follow-through on that protection is limited. There is no marriage and no civil-partnership regime: the 2018 referendum to amend the constitution failed on low turnout, and the Orthodox Church has opposed a civil-partnership bill since 2017. LGBTI organisations can register and operate.  Legal gender recognition exists and is court-based. In the Arian Mirzarafie-Ahi case, the Sector 6 Court of Bucharest ordered a new birth certificate reflecting the trans man's UK-recognised identity, and the Bucharest Tribunal rejected the appeals filed by the Cluj civil-status directorates, making the decision definitive in March 2026. ACCEPT Romania announced the outcome on Trans Day of Visibility and urges others who have changed their documents in another European Union member state to pursue transcription in Romania.  The legal anchor is the Court of Justice of the European Union's ruling of October 2024, reported by Reuters, that Romania infringed a transgender man's rights in the Mirzarafie-Ahi case, which concerns recognition of a UK gender recognition certificate in Romania. The ruling builds on the position that member states must transcribe intra-EU legal gender recognition.  A Council of Europe thematic review of January 2023, 'Hate Crimes and Other Hate Motivated Incidents Against LGBTI People in Romania', documents the national report on implementation of Recommendation CM/Rec(2010)5, covering the legal and policy framework, applicable European Court of Human Rights case-law and international standards.  Official hostility intensified during 2025. The ILGA-Europe Annual Review 2026 records that anti-LGBTI rhetoric rose through the presidential campaign: candidate Călin Georgescu declared himself 'against LGBTQ' in February, Prime Minister Ciolacu mocked gender-marker changes, and a Ploiești deputy mayor of AUR made further derogatory announcements. The National Audiovisual Council issued a public warning to B1 TV in August over anti-Pride 'provocation' framing after an ACCEPT complaint.  The ILGA-Europe and partners' submission to the EU 2025 Rule of Law Report, whose Romania chapter was authored by ACCEPT, found that eight of nine country submissions reported smear campaigns, disinformation and hate speech against LGBTI people, and cites the surge in anti-LGBTI narratives during the Romanian election period as the clearest example of rights-impacting rule-of-law erosion.  Public visibility carries visible risk. AP reported in June 2025 that tens of thousands marched on the twentieth anniversary of the Bucharest Pride march amid rising right-wing hostility toward LGBTQ+ Romanians.  The ILGA-Europe Annual Review 2024, covering 2023, records that the National Council for Combating Discrimination investigated printing houses that refused to print LGBT and gender-equality materials.

sources.title: European Court of Human Rights - 23 May 2023 Article 8 ruling
sources.documents: Finds Romania breaching Article 8 ECHR by not allowing same-sex couples to marry or register civil partnerships; documents lack of legal recognition despite 2018 high-court residency rulings.
sources.detail: Cited as 'On 23 May 2023 the European Court of Human Rights ruled that Romania is breaching article eight... by not allowing same-sex couples to marry or register civil partnerships.' Followed by PM Marcel Ciolacu Nov 2023 refusal. No URL visible.

sources.title: European Court of Human Rights - 2021 ruling on 20 February 2013 Museum incident
sources.documents: Documents enforcement failure and anti-LGBTQ incident: ~50 protesters stopped screening of 'The Kids Are All Right' at Museum of the Romanian Peasant shouting 'Death to the homosexuals', filming attendees; Court found violation of Article 8 and 11 and discrimination on sexual orientation for failure to conduct effective investigation.
sources.detail: Incident dated 'evening of 20 February' during LGBTQ History Month; ruling dated 'In 2021, the European Court of Human Rights ruled that Romania violated Article 8 and Article 11'. No URL visible.

sources.title: National Council for Combating Discrimination (CNCD) - 2000 anti-discrimination law enforcement
sources.documents: Rights machinery; 2000 Parliament law outlawing sexual orientation discrimination in employment, goods/services, housing, education, health, audiovisual, justice; CNCD fines, e.g., TAROM fined for refusing same-sex partners couples discounts Valentine's Day 2005 and ordered to rectify.
sources.detail: Cited as law 'among the most comprehensive in the European Union, has been successfully tested by the National Council for Combating Discrimination (CNCD)' with TAROM example. Also 2006 Penal Code amendments on incitement and aggravating circumstance. No URL visible.

sources.title: CNCD September 2007 MSM blood donation ruling and Ministry of Health January 2008 law
sources.documents: Documents discriminatory MSM blood ban and equality-body remedy; CNCD ruled ban illegal creating 'hostile, degrading, humiliating and offensive atmosphere for homosexuals' and ordered removal; Ministry issued new law Jan 2008 removing ban, not yet implemented.
sources.detail: Cited as 'in September 2007, Romania's National Council for Combating Discrimination ruled that this ban was illegal' and 'In January 2008... Ministry of Health released a new law'. No URL visible.

sources.title: EU Fundamental Rights Agency 2013 LGBT survey / ACCEPT 2010 survey
sources.documents: Documented prevalence of anti-LGBTQ discrimination/violence in Romania; FRA ranks Romania third after Croatia and Bulgaria, 21% attacked/threatened in past 5 years; ACCEPT 2010: 68.2% suffered discrimination/exclusion, >50% insulted, 30% threatened, streets 49.5% main site.
sources.detail: Cited as '2013 survey by the European Union's Fundamental Rights Agency' and 'survey done by ACCEPT association in 2010'. Also CNCD 3 April 2012 'Perceptions and Attitudes Regarding Discrimination' report. No URL visible.

name: Sudan
summary_text: Sudan is a jurisdiction in which gender nonconformity is itself a criminal offence. Article 152 of the Penal Code prohibits wearing clothing of the opposite sex, and the provision targets gender presentation rather than sexual conduct. A trans visitor whose appearance is read as incongruent with the sex recorded on their documents falls squarely within its scope, independent of any other behaviour.  Same-sex sexual activity between men and between women is also criminalised. The Human Dignity Trust country profile records a maximum sentence of life imprisonment, with the death penalty historically available for a third offence. Following the amendment adopted by Sudan's Sovereign Council in July 2020, the death penalty for homosexuality was removed and the maximum penalty for a third offence set at life imprisonment; the 100 lashes previously imposed for same-sex intimacy were abolished and a first offence carries up to five years' imprisonment.  The 2010 US State Department human rights report for Sudan records the then-applicable Article 148 provisions, which carried flogging and the death penalty. The same report documents extrajudicial killings, torture and other abuses under the Bashir government.  Sudan provides no legal gender recognition. Gender-affirming healthcare is legally constrained, the ongoing conflict further restricts access to it, and state reliance on Sunni fatwas blocks transition. Cairo 52's Sudan profile reports no arrest statistics specific to trans people, but does document state violence against LGBTQIA+ individuals, including extrajudicial killings.  Documentation by Bedayaa, the LGBTQI organisation for the Nile Valley, records daily struggles, discrimination and violence against LGBTQI people in Sudan rooted in societal gender and sexual norms. Rainbow Sudan, a Sudanese community magazine, records an organised local community presence, including history and analysis of LGBTI rights in Sudan and profiles of Sudanese LGBTI organisations.

sources.title: Criminal Act of 1991, Article 148 (as amended 2009)
sources.documents: Defines sodomy as anal sex illegal in Sudan whether same-sex or opposite-sex; legal basis for criminalization and prior capital/corporal punishment
sources.detail: Citation visible as 'Article 148 of the Criminal Act of 1991' and 'as amended in 2009' - no URL visible in text

sources.title: U.S. Department of State 2011 Human Rights Report on Sudan
sources.documents: Documents law prohibits sodomy but no reports of antisodomy laws being applied; no known LGBT organizations; official discrimination based on sexual orientation and gender identity; widespread societal discrimination; vigilantes targeted suspected gay men and lesbians for violent abuse and public demonstrations against homosexuality
sources.detail: Citation visible as "The U.S. Department of State's 2011 human rights report found that:" with quoted findings - no URL visible
